title: A spectral-norm generalization of the Böttcher-Wenzel inequality for rectangular matrices
statement:
Let $M_{m,n}(\mathbb{C})$ denote the space of complex $m\times n$ matrices. For a matrix, write $\|\cdot\|_F$ for the Frobenius norm, $\|\cdot\|_2$ for the spectral norm, and $\|A\|_{(2),2}$ for the norm appearing in the stated inequality. Let $A,C\in M_{m,n}(\mathbb{C})$ and $B\in M_{n,m}(\mathbb{C})$, where $m,n\geq 2$. **Spectral-norm generalization.**

$$
\|ABC-CBA\|^{2}_{F}\leq 2\|B\|^{2}_{2}\|A\|^{2}_{(2),2}\|C\|_{F}^{2}.
$$

This conjecture would generalize the Böttcher-Wenzel-type inequalities considered in the paper to the case in which the norm of $B$ is the spectral norm. It is based on numerical experiments; its general validity remains open.
references:
Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.17365

Status: no resolution is reported in the source (as of June 2025).

progress.summary:
Motoyuki Nobori posed this conjecture in 2025 for rectangular matrices with $m,n\geq 2$, based on numerical experiments. It asks whether the Böttcher--Wenzel-type bound remains valid when $B$ is measured by the spectral norm.

*[arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/html/2506.17365v2)*

**Known results**

- Nobori, 2025: the related bound with $\|C\|_2^2\|B\|_F^2$ is proved for all rectangular sizes.
- Nobori, 2025: the target-form inequality is proved when $m=1$ or $n=1$.
- Nobori, 2025: the related tensor bound is established when $\operatorname{rank}B\leq 2$, but this does not settle the conjecture for $m,n\geq 2$.

*[arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.17365)*

**Posted attempt**

A reader-written argument claims a complete proof for every $m,n\geq 1$, by decomposing a normalized $B$ into isometries or coisometries and applying square-matrix inequalities. It also claims a stronger tensor bound, but neither claim has been independently verified.

Current status (as of August 2026): Nobori’s edge cases and related rank-restricted results are settled, while the full conjecture has only an unverified complete-proof claim and remains mathematically unconfirmed.

*Caveats. The posted argument is unreviewed, and no corroborating paper, verification, counterexample, or retraction was found.*

solutions.body:
# The spectral-norm Böttcher--Wenzel conjecture for rectangular matrices

**Source and prior results.** Motoyuki Nobori, *A generalization of the Böttcher--Wenzel inequality for three rectangular matrices*, [Linear Algebra and its Applications 725 (2025), 135--144](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.laa.2025.07.005), Conjecture 3.1; freely available as [arXiv:2506.17365v2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.17365). The square-matrix estimates used below are established prior results, stated explicitly as equations (2) and (3) in that paper; see also K. M. R. Audenaert, [Linear Algebra and its Applications 432 (2010), 1126--1143](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.laa.2009.10.022), and A. Böttcher and D. Wenzel, [Linear Algebra and its Applications 429 (2008), 1864--1885](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.laa.2008.05.020). The new step is to deduce the full rectangular three-matrix conjecture from those square-matrix theorems by an explicit convex decomposition into isometries or coisometries.

Let

$$
A,C\in M_{m,n}(\mathbb C),
\qquad
B\in M_{n,m}(\mathbb C),
$$

and write

$$
\|A\|_{(2),2}^2
=
\sigma_1(A)^2+\sigma_2(A)^2,
$$

with a missing second singular value interpreted as zero. We prove, for every $m,n\ge1$,

$$
\boxed{
\|ABC-CBA\|_F^2
\le
2\|B\|_2^2\|A\|_{(2),2}^2\|C\|_F^2.
}
\tag{1}
$$

In particular, this proves Conjecture 3.1 for all complex rectangular matrices in its stated range $m,n\ge2$.

## 1. Every rectangular contraction is an explicit average of extremal isometries

The case $B=0$ is immediate. Otherwise, by homogeneity, replace $B$ by

$$
D=\frac{B}{\|B\|_2}.
$$

Put $p=\min\{m,n\}$ and choose a singular-value decomposition

$$
D=U\Sigma V^*,
\qquad
U\in U(n),
\qquad
V\in U(m),
\qquad
\Sigma_{ii}=s_i\in[0,1]
\quad(1\le i\le p),
\tag{2}
$$

where the remaining entries of the rectangular $n\times m$ matrix $\Sigma$ are zero.

For each sign vector

$$
\varepsilon=(\varepsilon_1,\ldots,\varepsilon_p)
\in\{-1,1\}^p,
$$

let $J_{\varepsilon}$ be the rectangular diagonal matrix with diagonal entries $\varepsilon_i$, and set

$$
\omega_{\varepsilon}
=
\prod_{i=1}^p\frac{1+\varepsilon_i s_i}{2},
\qquad
Q_{\varepsilon}=UJ_{\varepsilon}V^*.
\tag{3}
$$

The weights are nonnegative and satisfy

$$
\sum_{\varepsilon}\omega_{\varepsilon}=1,
\qquad
\sum_{\varepsilon}\omega_{\varepsilon}\varepsilon_i=s_i.
$$

Consequently

$$
D
=
\sum_{\varepsilon}
\omega_{\varepsilon}Q_{\varepsilon}.
\tag{4}
$$

If $n\ge m$, every summand is an isometry:

$$
Q_{\varepsilon}^*Q_{\varepsilon}=I_m.
\tag{5}
$$

If $n\le m$, every summand is a coisometry:

$$
Q_{\varepsilon}Q_{\varepsilon}^*=I_n.
\tag{6}
$$

The square case satisfies both identities. Thus no approximation, closure argument, or existence theorem for extreme points is needed.

## 2. The isometric case

Suppose $n\ge m$, and fix one summand $Q=Q_{\varepsilon}$ from (4). Form the square $n\times n$ matrices

$$
X=QA,
\qquad
Y=QC.
$$

Their commutator is exactly

$$
[X,Y]
=
QAQC-QCQA
=
Q(AQC-CQA).
\tag{7}
$$

Since $Q^*Q=I_m$, left multiplication by $Q$ preserves the Frobenius norm. It also preserves all singular values, because

$$
(QA)^*(QA)=A^*A.
$$

Hence

$$
\|[X,Y]\|_F
=\|AQC-CQA\|_F,
\qquad
\|X\|_{(2),2}=\|A\|_{(2),2},
\qquad
\|Y\|_F=\|C\|_F.
\tag{8}
$$

Apply the established square-matrix inequality, equation (2) of the source,

$$
\|[X,Y]\|_F^2
\le
2\|X\|_{(2),2}^2\|Y\|_F^2.
$$

Using (8) gives

$$
\|AQC-CQA\|_F
\le
\sqrt2\,\|A\|_{(2),2}\|C\|_F.
\tag{9}
$$

## 3. The coisometric case

Suppose $n\le m$ instead, so $QQ^*=I_n$. This time form the square $m\times m$ matrices

$$
X=AQ,
\qquad
Y=CQ.
$$

Then

$$
[X,Y]
=
AQCQ-CQAQ
=
(AQC-CQA)Q.
\tag{10}
$$

Right multiplication by $Q$ preserves the Frobenius norm. All singular values are again preserved, now because

$$
(AQ)(AQ)^*=AA^*.
$$

Therefore

$$
\|[X,Y]\|_F
=\|AQC-CQA\|_F,
\qquad
\|X\|_{(2),2}=\|A\|_{(2),2},
\qquad
\|Y\|_F=\|C\|_F.
$$

Applying the same established square inequality proves (9) in the coisometric case as well.

## 4. Averaging proves the conjecture

The generalized commutator is linear in its middle factor. Therefore (4), the triangle inequality, and (9) give

$$
\begin{aligned}
\|ADC-CDA\|_F
&=
\left\|
\sum_{\varepsilon}
\omega_{\varepsilon}
(AQ_{\varepsilon}C-CQ_{\varepsilon}A)
\right\|_F
\\
&\le
\sum_{\varepsilon}
\omega_{\varepsilon}
\|AQ_{\varepsilon}C-CQ_{\varepsilon}A\|_F
\\
&\le
\sqrt2\,\|A\|_{(2),2}\|C\|_F.
\end{aligned}
\tag{11}
$$

Multiplying by $\|B\|_2$ and squaring yields (1).

## 5. The stronger alternating-tensor bound also holds in every rank

The source also asks whether the stronger-looking consequence

$$
\|ABC-CBA\|_F^2
\le
\|B\|_2^2
\|A\otimes C-C\otimes A\|_F^2
\tag{12}
$$

holds. It verifies this when $\operatorname{rank}B\le2$ but leaves the unrestricted case unresolved.

Use precisely the same square matrices $X,Y$ as above. Isometric or coisometric multiplication preserves not only singular values and Frobenius norms, but also the Frobenius inner product:

$$
\langle X,Y\rangle_F
=
\langle A,C\rangle_F.
$$

The established square commutator estimate, equation (3) of the source, therefore gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\|AQC-CQA\|_F^2
&=
\|[X,Y]\|_F^2
\\
&\le
2\left(
\|X\|_F^2\|Y\|_F^2
-|\langle X,Y\rangle_F|^2
\right)
\\
&=
2\left(
\|A\|_F^2\|C\|_F^2
-|\langle A,C\rangle_F|^2
\right)
\\
&=
\|A\otimes C-C\otimes A\|_F^2.
\end{aligned}
\tag{13}
$$

Averaging the unsquared inequality exactly as in (11), then restoring $\|B\|_2$, proves (12) for arbitrary complex rectangular matrices and every rank of $B$.

By additionally exchanging $A$ and $C$, one obtains the simultaneous refinement

$$
\begin{aligned}
\|ABC-CBA\|_F^2
\le
2\|B\|_2^2
\min\Bigl\{
&\|A\|_{(2),2}^2\|C\|_F^2,
\\
&\|C\|_{(2),2}^2\|A\|_F^2,
\\
&\|A\|_F^2\|C\|_F^2
-|\langle A,C\rangle_F|^2
\Bigr\}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{14}
$$

The coefficient $2$ is sharp. In dimension $m=n=2$, take

$$
A=
\begin{pmatrix}
1&0
\\
0&-1
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
B=I_2,
\qquad
C=
\begin{pmatrix}
0&1
\\
0&0
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Then

$$
\|ABC-CBA\|_F^2=4,
\qquad
\|B\|_2^2=1,
\qquad
\|A\|_{(2),2}^2=2,
\qquad
\|C\|_F^2=1,
$$

so equality holds in both (1) and (12). Padding these matrices with zero rows and columns gives sharp examples in every rectangular dimension with $m,n\ge2$.
